newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU monetary panel meets on single currency.
newsitem.headline: EU monetary panel meets on single currency.

text.p: The European Union's monetary committee began a meeting on Tuesday to hammer out the details of a budget stability pact for countries joining a single currency in 1999.

EU monetary officials said the group, comprised of national treasury and central bank officials, will also focus on a new Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) that links the single currency, the euro, to currencies outside monetary union.
Rounding out the discussion will be the legal underpinnings of monetary union, with an emphasis on how a legal framework for the euro can be obtained in advance of the 1999 start date.

At an informal gathering of EU finance ministers and central bankers in Dublin last month, it was agreed that a stability pact among EMU members should exist, but several details were left for the monetary committee to resolve.

Among them is the rather difficult task of defining the economic circumstances under which a government could avoid sanctions should its deficit rise above three percent of gross domestic product (GDP), the Maastricht treaty's proposed limit.
Many believe it will be difficult to find a precise definition of so-called exceptional and temporary economic circumstances -- in other words, a sharp economic downturn.
Another issue concerns the time period between when a government is cited as having an excessive deficit and when it would actually have to pay a fine.

There is also debate over the level of fines a government would face, although many seem to be leaning towards the European Commission's proposal -- an initial 0.2 or 0.3 percent of a country's GDP, followed by 0.1 percent of total output for every percentage point above the three percent level.
A maximum ceiling of 0.5 percent of output is also proposed.
There is less controversy over a revamped ERM, with the European Monetary Institute, Europe's nascent central bank, having made considerable progress on defining the outline of such a system.
One outstanding issue concerns the degree to which a European Central Bank would intervene to support currencies outside the grid when they come under speculative attack.
On a legal framework for the single currency, there is agreement that the most urgent legal points of concern for financial markets should be brought into legal force quickly.

These are the single currency's name, the continuity of contracts after January 1, 1999, a one-for-one conversion rate between and Ecu-basket of currencies and the euro, and a rule for sub-divisions of the euro.
The monetary committee will consider a Commission plan on how to do this within the bounds of the Maastricht treaty.
The objective is to have enough progress on all three areas in time for a summit of EU leaders in December.
